title: Formal Languages and Automata Theory
description: Words, languages and regular expressions; deterministic and nondeterministic finite automata; the pumping lemma, closure and decision properties and the Chomsky hierarchy; context-free grammars and normal forms; and pushdown automata. Built from the CSC 351 course book (Study Sessions 1 to 11).

topics.title: Words, Alphabets and Languages
topics.summary: A word is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet, and a language is a set of words. Words and languages are combined by concatenation, powers, reversal and the Kleene star and plus.
subtopics: Alphabets, words and the empty word ε
Finite, cofinite, empty and singleton languages
Σ*, Σ+, complement and language operations

topics.title: Regular Expressions and Regular Languages
topics.summary: A regular expression defines a language using union, concatenation and the Kleene star; the languages so defined are the regular languages. Algebraic laws simplify expressions, and every regular expression has an equivalent finite automaton.
subtopics: Building expressions: L(E + F), L(EF), L(E*)
Algebraic laws: identity, annihilator, distributive, idempotent
Converting between regular expressions and automata

topics.title: Deterministic Finite Automata
topics.summary: A deterministic finite automaton is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) that reads a string symbol by symbol and accepts it if it ends in an accept state. DFAs are designed for a language, and minimised by merging equivalent states.
subtopics: Designing a DFA for a language

topics.title: Nondeterministic Finite Automata
topics.summary: An NFA may have zero, one or many transitions for a symbol, and ε-transitions that consume no input; it accepts if any branch ends in an accept state. Every NFA and ε-NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA.
subtopics: Formal definition: δ: Q × Σε → P(Q)
Converting an ε-NFA to an NFA
Equivalence of DFA, NFA and ε-NFA

topics.title: Properties of Regular Languages and the Chomsky Hierarchy
topics.summary: The pumping lemma shows that languages such as {0^n 1^n} are not regular, and regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement and more. The Chomsky hierarchy ranks languages, grammars and machines from Type 3 to Type 0.
subtopics: The pumping lemma for regular languages
Proving a language is not regular
Decision problems: membership, emptiness, finiteness, equivalence
Closure of each class under union, intersection and complement

topics.title: Context-Free Grammars and Normal Forms
topics.summary: A context-free grammar of terminals, non-terminals, productions and a start symbol generates a context-free language; derivations and parse trees show how. Grammars may be ambiguous, and can be simplified and put into Chomsky or Greibach normal form.
subtopics: Components and formal definition of a CFG
Removing useless, unit and null productions

topics.title: Pushdown Automata
topics.summary: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton with a stack, which lets it recognise context-free languages such as {0^n 1^n}. It accepts by final state or by empty stack, and PDAs and CFGs describe the same languages.
subtopics: Input tape, control unit and stack
Transitions a, b → c and instantaneous descriptions
Acceptance by final state and by empty stack
